T1: Musicians will adopt hearing protection if it preserves sound quality and comfort, leading to higher willingness to pay for premium features. Who benefits: Musicians who need hearing protection for practice and performance. Why behaviour changes: Current barriers include impact on listening to music and performing; a product that mitigates these barriers would increase adoption. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge premium prices for models with advanced sound preservation technology and market directly to musicians through specialized channels. Assumptions: Musicians are willing to pay more for hearing protection that does not compromise sound quality; Hellberg can develop or source technology that preserves sound quality; Musicians will discover and purchase Hellberg products through targeted marketing. Predictions: In a test offering a musician-focused hearing protection model, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard model; Surveyed musicians will rate sound quality preservation as a key purchase criterion.

T2: Parents will purchase hearing protection for children if it is positioned as safe for school and hobby activities, leading to repeat purchases and brand loyalty. Who benefits: Parents of children aged 3-12 who engage in school, hobby, or recreational activities. Why behaviour changes: Parents seek safe, comfortable hearing protection for children; a product marketed specifically for children's activities addresses this need. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell through retail channels targeting parents, offer multi-pack or subscription options, and build brand recognition in the children's segment. Assumptions: Parents are willing to pay for child-specific hearing protection; Hellberg can design a product that meets safety and comfort expectations for children; Retail distribution reaches parents who buy for children. Test "Musician vs Parent Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to either a musician-focused product description (emphasizing sound preservation and comfort for performance) or a children-focused product description (emphasizing safety for school/hobby activities). They are asked to indicate likelihood to purchase on a 1-10 scale and whether they would recommend to others.. Sample: 200 participants: 100 musicians (recruited via music forums) and 100 parents of children aged 3-12 (recruited via parenting sites). Each participant sees only one product description.. Measure: Average purchase intent score (1-10) for each group. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (EUR) on a 5-point scale.. Predictions: T1: Musicians will show higher purchase intent for the musician-focused description than parents do for the same description.; T2: Parents will show higher purchase intent for the children-focused description than musicians do for the same description.. Decision rule: If musicians' average intent for musician description >= 7 and parents' average intent for children description >= 7, proceed to develop differentiated propositions for both segments. If either group's intent < 6, reconsider investment. If both groups show high intent for both. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for musicians first, as evidence suggests sound quality preservation is a key barrier to adoption. The musician segment shows clearer pain points (impact on listening/performing) that a product can address. The children segment (T2) relies on company claims without independent validation of parent willingness to pay or repeat purchase behavior. Prioritize the musician use Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test result that measures packing errors, not consumer demand or product adoption. It bears no relevance to T1's claim about musicians adopting hearing protection for sound quality preservation. The theory remains unchanged. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for musicians first, focusing on sound quality preservation and comfort during performance. The evidence from independent studies (couth-2022-musicians) identifies clear barriers (impact on listening/performing) that a product can address. The children segment (T2) relies on company claims without independent validation of parent willingness to pay or repeat purchase. Target customer: Early-career musicians who need hearing protection for practice and performance. Value proposition: Hearing protection that preserves sound quality and comfort, enabling musicians to protect their hearing without compromising their musical experience. Favoured theory: T1. Uncertainty: The test has not been run yet; willingness to pay and actual purchase behavior remain unverified. The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) is irrelevant to consumer demand.. Would change if: The test shows low purchase intent for musicians (<6/10); Independent evidence shows musicians are unwilling to pay a premium for sound preservation; Hellberg cannot source or develop the required sound preservation technology. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
